briefing.headline: The simulation predicts the three-day office rule would increase leavers over the next 12 months by about 40%, from 657 to 893, or roughly 236 extra departures out of 5,000 staff, with overall sentiment negative (-0.77 on a -2 to +2 scale).
briefing.most_at_risk: Long-commute employees react worst (+54% leaving versus +20% for short commuters), followed by caregivers (+50%) and managers (+47%), because an extra day in Bengaluru traffic, on top of late client calls, costs them hours each week while competitors still offer hybrid work.
risks: Long commuters are 60% of the workforce (3,000 people), and their voices say they will 'quietly look around' rather than resign right away, so losses may arrive steadily over the year instead of as a visible spike you can react to early.
The shuttle only runs on main routes, and several long-commute employees said its value depends on whether it covers their route; if it does not, the main mitigation fails for the group most at risk.
Caregivers are counting on the exception process. Those turned down say they will start job hunting, so a strict or slow HR response could turn the +50% caregiver figure into actual departures.
design_changes: Find out where staff actually live before announcing, then publish the shuttle routes and expand them to cover the largest long-commute clusters, so people know on day one whether it helps them.
Make it explicit that late US and Europe client calls can be taken from home, for example by letting people leave early on office days, so a third office day does not also mean a late-night commute.

Open the caregiving and health exception window now and publish clear criteria, so requests are decided before the policy starts rather than in the first weeks; consider a lighter version (such as two days) for very long commutes.
briefing.confidence: medium, because the direction is consistent (every group shows higher leaving, and the voices back the long-commute and caregiver pattern), but with only about two modelled voices per group, treat the +40% and the subgroup gaps as rough ranges, especially the manager figure, since the manager voices sampled sound fairly calm.
